Industry News: Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan.
  • In a recent development, taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character.
  • Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

In a recent development, taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Recent findings suggest that the 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka’s projected route across Taiwan.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition proposal includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he plans to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

Tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

Recent findings suggest that during a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

In a recent development, on a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

According to recent reports, tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Industry observers note that yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

In a recent development, interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#33708. Breaking: Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1845 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest.
  • Sources indicate that it was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort.
  • Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

Sources indicate that it was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

Recent findings suggest that the expedition itself came from a merger of two prepares. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

According to recent reports, the Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times.

The Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia.

According to recent reports, base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later mentioned it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

According to recent reports, the Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

Industry observers note that the 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com.

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

In a recent development, major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

In a recent development, according to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt mentioned that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he stated. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com.

After the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They said that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

In a recent development, many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group said the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

Mazeaud’s radio message remarked that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that according to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later said that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He said they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

Roberts later remarked weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Industry observers note that roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

In a recent development, haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He noted that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura said that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

Axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt remarked the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

It has been revealed that the problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original blueprint of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth stated the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Sources indicate that memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

Tech Report: Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3374 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “This is absolute madness,” stated a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England.
  • The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.
  • According to recent reports, when Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“This is absolute madness,” stated a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

According to recent reports, when Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

Industry observers note that bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he said: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”.

Through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby.

It has been revealed that while serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to Upcoming York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at Fresh York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

“That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby demonstrated nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

He gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

In a recent development, 2001, the Darien Gap. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The Newly introduced York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”.

According to recent reports, the first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

Industry observers note that after making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

North America. Photo: Karl Bushby.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

In March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Sources indicate that wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The Fresh York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”.

They made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Industry observers note that russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

Sources indicate that the years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

When visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Sources indicate that bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Sources indicate that the distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

In a recent development, the arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

Sources indicate that he lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:.

According to recent reports, I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

The passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

Industry observers note that while Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

When his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

In a recent development, they later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”.

According to recent reports, in various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

Industry observers note that “The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”.

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”.

Recent findings suggest that he has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

In a recent development, at the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

In a recent development, visa complications and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a new plan. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

It has been revealed that back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

Recent findings suggest that the remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

According to recent reports, he made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next glitch. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

Recent findings suggest that karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube.

In a recent development, as he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

According to recent reports, still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a initiative for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

French rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

According to recent reports, the crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

It has been revealed that after 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The Upcoming York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he mentioned. “It’s about to abruptly end.”.

According to recent reports, he is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

Industry observers note that one substantial question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

Karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube.

In a recent development, it might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

According to recent reports, with just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

According to recent reports, then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

In a recent development, now that he has to confront a upcoming question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”.

Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less.
  • In a recent development, no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long.
  • It has been revealed that the climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

In a recent development, no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

It has been revealed that the climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

According to recent reports, vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:.

We know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to newly introduced conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

According to recent reports, the fresh snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:.

Industry observers note that it is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

On Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

According to recent reports, so far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

Recent findings suggest that I find it surprising that so many BH members — including some who have been here for years — would favor an approach that intentionally excludes newly public companies until they meet S&P’s rules.The arguments are usually that these companies are too small to matter, not yet profitable, overhyped, or not seasoned enough.I’m saying all of that except too small to matter. The point is that historically those overvalued companies used to join the indexes at positions too small to matter, and that was a good thing. They needed to work their way up to higher weights. Now, these companies are staying private much longer and becoming truly enormous before going public. All while playing a different game than public firms of similar size when it comes to actual business profits.But how do you know those companies are overvalued? 💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.
  • The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies.
  • Recent findings suggest that as shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time.

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

Recent findings suggest that as shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Industry observers note that vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from New Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

#33700. Upcoming Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (633 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Upcoming Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border.
  • Industry observers note that the pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif.
  • Recent findings suggest that they placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

Industry observers note that the pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

Recent findings suggest that they placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health challenges. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

It has been revealed that from the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

According to recent reports, attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

Recent findings suggest that in late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

In a recent development, this was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

Sources indicate that from the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

#33699. Breaking: Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (424 w)

Breaking: Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (424 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River.
  • This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river.
  • Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram.

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

According to recent reports, though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

It has been revealed that but according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this notable riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#33698. Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2600 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it was a fitful, fretful night.
  • On one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever.
  • Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  46,975 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  28:21.

Recent findings suggest that it was a fitful, fretful night. It continued to rain for a while, off and on, and the wind came up again, continuing throughout the night. The whole time I was worrying about staying warm, staying dry, and making the fewest possible excursions outside to pee.

On one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever. I picked up my poncho, which was just lying on the ground soaking wet, and I draped it over a pine tree, so it looked like a scarecrow. Or maybe a scare-bear?

Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.

Indeed, the morning came. I got up reasonably early, at 6:30, and had breakfast in my tent. In my warm, now semi-dry tent.

The good thing was that the rain had stopped. The poncho I stood up as a decoy in the night, was now wind dried. So, I used it for staging. I put it on the wet ground and pulled all of my stuff out of the tent and placed it on the dry poncho. If things were dry, they stayed dry; if wet, at least they didn’t get any wetter.

Things looked a LOT better at my camp site in the morning!

This mattered, because I had a lot of wet stuff. I had a wet hoodie. I had wet shorts, wet socks, and wet shoes.

After evacuating the tent, I took it down. Thanks to the wind, the fly – that had been soaking wet — was basically dry. But the ground cloth and the bottom of the tent were very wet.

It has been revealed that what to do? I could either dry them and be done with it, or pack them wet, and dry them later. While thinking about this, I put them on logs, and laid them out to dry, so that my indecision became a decision. When the sun peeked out a little, I put them on rocks. Yes, it ate up a lot of time, but when they were finally dry, I could stop worrying about that matter and just hike.

Recent findings suggest that at 9:00 a.m. I set off. I was wearing wet-cold shoes, wet-cold shorts, wet-cold gloves, a wet-cold hoodie, and a wet-cold hat. Only one thing was not wet and cold:  I decided to go ahead and use my dry socks. I hoped that my shoes were just moist and not soaking wet, and my dry socks would be a barrier to that moisture. That plan worked out pretty well.

Sources indicate that because it was cold in the aftermath of the storm, I started with a lot of energy, to get my blood flowing. I needed it too, for the trail sang one refrain:  up, up, up, and up.

Looking back at the hill I climbed — but at least I was warm, and getting dry!

In a recent development, by the time I reached the ridge, and looked down on Garnet Lake, I was mostly dry and all warmed up. Then I got lost.

I could see Garnet Lake, I just couldn’t see how to GET there!

According to recent reports, I knew I had to go east, and I spotted a little trail to the east, so I started down that trail until it kind of disappeared. Then I spent about ten minutes wandering around up there, trying to find my way, unable to believe the east-going trail was a false trail. Finally, I retraced my steps far enough to notice a separate west-going trail. That was counterintuitive, but it was the correct trail, because it eventually looped around, lower down, and went east, as I knew it should.

I name this “One Pine Tree Island” in Garnet Lake.

Walking along the shore of Garnet Lake I envisioned what might have happened if I had made it to this destination in the storm the day before. I could imagine myself, struggling with my tent in the rain, and having a huge gust of wind lift the tent like a beach ball and deposit it in the middle of the lake! It would have been bad! Yes, hilarious, but bad.

To reinforce the power of the storm the day before, this was Ninja Queen’s  description of her experience, as she sent it to me via text, with almost no editing:.

“…you can imagine how horribly wrong the day of the storm went for me. I should have hunkered down early like most other hikers had, but I foolishly trusted my (Garmin) InReach weather forecast a little too much, went over Island Pass (a tiny pass but a pass nonetheless) when the storm hit full force two hours early. It was bad. Really, really bad. The trail flooded very swiftly, got washed out and started diverging in multiple directions from the torrential downpour. They were ankle-deep and I kept losing the actual trail; it had become mini rivers at that point. Needless to say, I got wetted out through and through, shivering intensely, my hands no longer functioning, unable to take another step. I ended up setting up camp on some random flat-ish spot over some vegetation that also started pooling water. I was so afraid my tent was going to get flooded. Almost everything inside the tent was wet and muddy as well, though I was able to change into dry sleep clothes and sleeping bag, thanks to my nylofume pack liners. It took me a couple of hours, but I eventually warmed up in the bag, cooked and ate food inside (bears were the last of my worries at this point) and drank as little water as possible so I wouldn’t have to go out until the next morning. Putting back on cold, dripping wet clothes the next morning felt torture-adjacent; something I hope I’ll never have to go through again.”.

According to recent reports, “It gave me a small chuckle seeing other hikers also emerge from non-established tent sites the next morning. I quickly learned what I went through was not a typical rainstorm experience. Almost everyone I talked to said it had been one of the worst storms they’ve seen on trail. One guy, a firefighter, told me this was far worse than the hurricane weather he had caught on the AT (Appalachian Trail) a few years back. Now I felt like a survivor, instead of feeling like a fair weather backpacker who crumbled at the slightest hint of bad weather.”.

I filled up my water at the bridge where a stream exits the lake. There were a lot of folks around there, laying out their tents to dry from the storm. It was surprising, and a little disturbing, to see how much foam, and even spume-like foam, was on Garnet Lake, which looks otherwise pristine. I didn’t ask anybody about it at the time, who would I ask?

But later I Googled AI and discovered:  “…foam usually forms naturally when decaying plants, algae, and organic debris release compounds that lower water surface tension, and wind or wave action whips air into bubbles.”  In other words, the wind from the storm had produced the foam, not some giant industrial complex just out of view!

According to recent reports, I continued up, from Garnet to beautiful Ruby Lake, then to Emerald Lake, and finally the Thousand Islands Lake. This was an exceptionally scenic stretch.

I think this was Ruby Lake… if the water were sparkling red, it would be easier to tell!

Of course this was Thousand Islands Lake — with a pretty terrific backdrop!

There was very little elevation gain from there to Island Pass. Once the trail reached the ridge on the opposite side of the lake it seemed to stay at a mostly constant elevation for a very long time. The longer it went on, the more I wondered, “Pass? Is there really a pass up here somewhere? Where?”.

No pass, but a pretty cool-looking mushroom!

How can you tell when you have reached a pass? When you can see the other side of the mountain. It felt like that was never going to happen.

Sources indicate that finally, it was getting to be lunchtime. I decided to sit next to a charming little pond up there, and to eat my lunch.

Basically, I ate half of the food that I had brought as lunch, saving the other half for “second lunch.”  But afterwards, I just didn’t feel like I had much energy. Even finally reaching the edge did not inspire me. I saw the edge of the pass and started heading down, but my legs felt heavy. My legs felt like limp spaghetti.

In a recent development, when your legs don’t want to go, you need your brain to execute an override. So, I forced myself to keep going. Finally, I stopped again and made myself a second lunch in that sort of halfway space between Island Pass and Donohue Pass. About five miles separated them and Donohue represented the entrance to Yosemite National Park.

A dead tree by a stream; dead is how I felt before second lunch!

After lunch I had more energy, and I continued.

According to recent reports, throughout the JMT, whenever I approached a location where I knew there was a pass in the ridgeline, I always looked up to see if I could figure out where it might be. “Is that it? No, is that it? Wait, is that it?”  I suspect most hikers do this.

According to recent reports, with Donohue Pass it was hidden around the corner of an extending hump of rock, so of course I guessed wrong. Just short of the summit, I saw a full backpack about 25 yards from the trail. That seemed strange and I looked around. Was someone off going to the bathroom? There was nothing but silence. I continued on, but with a nagging worry for whoever was not connected with their pack.

When I arrived on top, at 11,066 feet elevation, I was all alone. In honor of my son Gabriel, who coined the pun, I bellowed, “YO! SEMITE!!!”  I got no answer, not even an echo. Even so, I was in Yosemite. It felt strange to be just a few days from the end — barring injury, of course.

Sources indicate that as I headed down from Donohue, I thought, “On the one hand, I don’t want to set up in the dark. But there are not too many campsites up here and, of course, I am a couple of miles behind schedule because of the storm.”  I resolved to take a chance and push it a little bit.

As a result, the riverside campsites just below Donohue Pass did not tempt me; they were filling up in any case.

The first camp north of Donohue Pass was by this ugly little lake….

Instead, I descended rapidly and with determination. As I did, I encountered a group heading southbound, up to the pass behind me. One young man was not carrying a pack. Apparently, he had come down to assist his family in making the ascent. He told me, “I left my pack up near the Pass so that I would not be encumbered in helping my family.”  I breathed deeply; mystery solved.

The first stretch went through rocky scree. I asked the mountain gods, “Why is there so much rocky scree?”  They rewarded me with forest.

See the meadow, far below there? My campsite was somewhere down there….

According to recent reports, the descent continued sharply through the woods, and I passed several gorgeous camping sites near the steeply dropping steam. Each time I told myself, “No! Not yet!” and then each time I regretted it, and wondered if I would ever find another spot, after that perfect one I had just rejected.

Recent findings suggest that at last, the steep downhill tapered off, and I reached the valley at the bottom. The stream, now wider and larger, and the trail continued to parallel each other. The going became easier for both the water and my legs.

In a recent development, following the river there were a few more possible places. As the sun slipped behind the mountains, but still with plenty of light, I saw a knoll overlooking a wide meadow. On that knoll was a lovely camping spot. I was home for the night.

The sun remains on the hillside, even as it gets dark in the valley.

My dinner was rice and beans and chicken, Santa Fe style. I let it soak as I pitched my tent and arranged my site. I let it soak some more as I explored higher up, in the giant granite boulders above the site, to find a cat hole location. It soaked still longer as I dug the hole in preparation for the next morning. But then, with no chores left to do, I got impatient. I ate.

According to recent reports, the dish was very well-seasoned, very tasty. This was certainly a meal I would recommend having again, on another hike, in another place. But rice takes a long time to absorb water when cold-soaking, and I didn’t wait long enough. The flavors were great, but the rice was… crunchy. I didn’t care much. It had been a strenuous day, coming the day after the intense storm. I was tired and hungry and starved for calories. I ate it all with gusto, crunch and all!

I was feeling good. It was a long day, and I had crossed two passes. I was finally in Yosemite. I haven’t mentioned the aftermath of my fall too much in recent posts, but my ribs were finally hurting less. My wrist was still a problem, to some degree, but it was functional.

The next day, I would be passing through Tuolumne Meadow. There I would either get a permit for Half Dome, or I would not. If I did, I probably had three days of hiking left. If I did not, then it would likely be two days. I had well under forty miles to go.

As the twilight deepened, I was loving my campsite facing the open meadow. I was proud of the mileage I had achieved, after the shortened day in the storm. My eyes closed and I welcomed blissful sleep.

#33697. Industry News: Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (604 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route.
  • The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023.
  • Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Initiative B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

It has been revealed that the team mentioned that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”.

Sources indicate that A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza.

Sources indicate that they reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”.

In a recent development, one of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza.

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

Sources indicate that the situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet.

According to recent reports, there was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

In a recent development, nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet.

It has been revealed that “We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”.

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet.

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”.

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza said.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

The Spanish team sent us the video below summarizing the climb.

#33696. The Long Rainy Road

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Long Rainy Road

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks.
  • Any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours.
  • A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks. That is about to change.

Any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours. The first domino to fall. Now I had to hope that it wouldn’t be actively raining when it comes time to pack up camp. It promptly becomes impossible to keep my pack dry in such a scenario, how do I keep the pack dry when I have to disassemble and roll up my only dry place? Lucky for me, when light first broke the rain noise had stopped. I patted the walls of my tent to dispel some of the leftover water and checked the time. 6:17AM. I decided to save breakfast for later and go straight into packing up so I could check the sunrise and then get to hiking before the precipitation inevitably arrived. At The Pinnacle my instincts were correct, nothing but a small patch of orange glow that could have been a candy wrapper blowing in the wind. I was unbothered, any day where there is rain but I don’t have to pack up in the rain is alright with me. With rain imminent I chose to throw on my poncho, though that decision was partially based on the chillier than expected morning and early start time.

A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock. Conveniently, I can save a few rocky steps by taking the clear driveway past the the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories. Its worth mentioning that the society provides a privy and trash can that can be used by hikers. They do ask that hikers don’t camp on the property or use flashlights, for obvious reasons. At the far end of the site I arrived at Pulpit Rock, which still offered a nice view despite the cloudy skies.

Recent findings suggest that from there I didn’t hesitate to use the road down from the observatories all the way down to the Windsor Furnace Shelter. I had a quick breakfast and got back on trail before 8:30AM. Hardly any rain had fallen, I wondered if I’d again be getting lucky with the weather and get all the way back to my van without getting soaked. I pushed hard to get the 5 or so miles to Port Clinton done. I knew the steep leafy trail awaited me and I was holding my breathe to get through that section before any heavy rain arrived – it would not be fun going up that section if the trail was steep, leafy, and turning into a stream all at the same time.

In a recent development, remarkably, the rain continued to hold off. I got closer and closer to Port Clinton, slowly realizing that the 60% chance of rain I saw for nearly every hour the day was landing in the 40% zone at least to start the day. I made it down the trail into town, back across the Schuykill River, and through the train yard. I charged up the hill, still expecting rain at any moment. The climb up proved tough, but not as treacherous as the climb down. This is the one time working against gravity actually works with you. Soon I was back on the ridge and heading toward the gravel road that would take me all the way back to my van on route 183. I thought that if the rain fell there it wouldn’t be a major deal, the hiking would at least be easy.

The Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories near Pulpit Rock.

Breakfast at the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

A steep climb coming out of the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

I was just starting to think of the impossible. Could I get all the way back to my van without any serious rain? It would take about 3 and half hours to get all the way back to my van hiking at full bore on the gravel road. I didn’t have any stops to make, I was in a straight race with nature. My hopes slowly grew and then, with a single sound, were completely erased. On a downhill section of the road I heard thunder ahead. The forecast didn’t say anything about thunderstorms, but I suppose it didn’t say it would be dry for the better part of the morning either. I was fairly exposed on the road, there was going to be rain, and soon it came. I pulled my poncho back over me, I had stashed it over my shoulders during the climb to stay cool, staying dry was the priority now.

In a recent development, the wind blew and the rain progressed swiftly from light drizzle to a steady downpour. The thunder bellowed louder and I began seeing flashes of lightning. The the rain started to feel sharp on my exposed hands. My gloves aren’t waterproof so it isn’t really worth it wear them in the rain. The rain had become freezing rain. Then it became hail the size of Nerds candy. The hail only lasted a few minutes, but the rain continued on. Although the day was in the mid 40s, the rain was ice cold. As soon as the rain became heavy my shoes and socks flooded. All I could do was shake my head and laugh, I had finally run out of luck, and things were regressing to the mean, emphasis on mean.

According to recent reports, none of the surprisingly severe weather slowed me down. I was determined to get back to my van and get dry. The rain continued for almost 2 hours. When it did finally stop, I noticed that the water drops on the trees appeared frozen in place. It looked like ice hanging on the branches and made it look a lot like I was hiking on a rainy, cold winter afternoon. For good, measure, the sun decided to come out with about 30 minutes left. A nice thought, but it was going to take more than a few rays of sunlight to dry out my shoes.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

It’s hard to see in the picture, but the scene had gotten considerably more wintery.

Near the end of the hike, the sun comes out.

Total: 24.4 miles, 45,270 steps.

I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu.
  • Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.
  • “Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”.

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

According to recent reports, the fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Recent findings suggest that satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung mentioned he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Sources indicate that tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who blueprint to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:.

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change swiftly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.
